solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Most unbalanced club matches end in rout

parts.note: a bat is a club used in cricket or baseball
in sport, ties are matches, especially cup fixtures

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A football fan grumbles that the most lopsided games end with one club routed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unbalanced' looks like a comment on mismatched teams, but it means mentally unbalanced; TIES is the British word for knockout fixtures.
explanation.definitionFit: Batty is informal for crazy, and the superlative describes someone the craziest of all.

clue.text: Fine baked goods silly chef's stuffing bacon in

indicators.note: silly means foolish or disordered, so the letters fall into a fresh order
stuffing is what sits inside, so only the inner letters of the word are taken

parts.note: the two middle letters of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A daft chef is stuffing bacon into fancy pastries, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: The final 'in' is part of the letters to rearrange, not a link: HE plus BACON plus IN gives BONE CHINA. 'Baked goods' suggests a bakery, but the goods are fired in a kiln.
explanation.definitionFit: Porcelain is fired in a kiln, so fine tableware made with bone ash is literally a set of baked goods.

clue.text: Name best applied to York Minster, initially

parts.note: top means the very best
something applied to a surface is on it

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each word gives only its opening letter

parts.note: the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone decides which title suits York Minster, the great cathedral in northern England.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a fitting example: York Minster is itself a place name.
explanation.definitionFit: A toponym is a word that is the label of a place, such as a town or river.

clue.text: Part of upper spine fused — time to separate it?

indicators.note: to separate a thing is to come between its parts, so one letter goes in the middle
fused things are melted down and set in a new form, so the letters are recast

parts.note: taken as written
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A medical question about fused vertebrae in the upper back: is it time to separate them?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upper spine' looks like anatomy, but the definition breaks after 'upper', the top part of a shoe; 'it' is the rearranged spine, split by T.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper is the top section of a shoe, and the instep is the part covering the arch of the foot.

clue.text: Unfairly blame head after second attack

indicators.note: after says the following piece is placed behind the one before, fixing their order

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a cape is a headland
to go at someone is to attack them

explanation.surface: A boss is wrongly blamed after a second assault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' looks like a person in charge; here it is a headland, such as Cape Horn.
explanation.definitionFit: To scapegoat someone is to make them carry the blame for others' wrongdoing, used here as a verb.

clue.text: Mark and The Times in meeting connected with competition puzzle

indicators.note: in places these pieces inside another word, which wraps round them

parts.note: a bee is a gathering for a contest, as in a spelling bee
M is the abbreviation for the German mark
the newspaper speaking of itself says us

explanation.surface: A notice about a gathering connected with the newspaper's prize crossword.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Competition puzzle' looks like one phrase, the prize crossword; the definition is just the last word, used as a verb. The Times setters use US for the paper itself.
explanation.definitionFit: To bemuse is to perplex or confuse, which is what puzzling someone does.

clue.text: Throne bishop is on by mistake

indicators.note: in a down entry, sitting on something means coming above it, which sets the order

parts.note: B is the chess notation for bishop
the throne is a jokey name for the toilet, the loo in British slang
per means by, as in per post

explanation.surface: A bishop has been seated on the throne by accident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throne' suggests a cathedral seat for the bishop; it is the toilet, LOO in British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A blooper is an embarrassing error, especially a broadcasting slip or gaffe.

clue.text: Need SIM or mobile update?

indicators.note: mobile means able to move, so the letters move into another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A phone user wonders whether a new SIM card or a whole new phone is needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile' looks like the phone itself, but it is the signal to rearrange the letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: To modernise is to bring something up to date, the same verb as update.

clue.text: Expand free entertainment setting aside area in school

indicators.note: in puts the remainder inside another word that surrounds it

parts.note: SCH is the abbreviation for school

indicators.note: setting something aside removes it, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: a treat is something enjoyable paid for by another
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A school widens its free activities by giving up a space.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage a treat is something paid for by someone else, so 'free entertainment' is fair; SCH is a standard crossword abbreviation for school.
explanation.definitionFit: To stretch is to extend or enlarge something, a straightforward synonym for the verb.

clue.text: Fluff pot on the double?

indicators.note: doubling something over folds it back on itself, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: a pan is a cooking pot

explanation.surface: An order to finish a pot shot, or mess one up, at speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the double' normally means quickly; here it is read as doubling back.
explanation.definitionFit: Nap is the raised fuzzy surface on cloth such as velvet, the soft fibres one might call fluff.

clue.text: One climbing frame that's come off the back of a lorry?

definitions.text: One climbing frame that's come off the back of a lorry?

parts.words: One climbing frame that's come off the back of a lorry?
parts.note: surface reading: a child's climbing frame of dubious origin, as goods that fell off a lorry are stolen
setter's reading: a worker who climbs a frame of poles and boards, unloaded from a truck at a building site

explanation.surface: Someone is offered a cut-price playground climbing frame of suspicious origin.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, goods that 'fell off the back of a lorry' are stolen; here the frame really was unloaded from a lorry, and 'one climbing' is a person.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesperson who erects the temporary pole structures on buildings climbs them as part of the job.

clue.text: Fraud never twitched, meeting organiser

parts.note: a con is a swindle

indicators.note: a twitch is a jerky movement, so the letters are jolted out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cool con artist kept a straight face while meeting the event organiser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fraud' looks like a person who stays calm; it is the swindle itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A convener is the person who calls people together and arranges a gathering or committee.

clue.text: Function requiring division by one to give equivalence

indicators.note: dividing something splits it so another piece can sit in the gap

parts.note: a function is a social gathering
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A maths exercise in which a function must be divided by one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Function' and 'division' sound mathematical, but the function is a social occasion split open by I.
explanation.definitionFit: Parity means being equal in status or value, so it matches equivalence as a noun.

clue.text: Foot whatever's left of injured American's medical bills

indicators.note: the left side of a word is where it begins, so only opening letters are kept

parts.note: the first letters of the four words

explanation.surface: An injured American pays their hospital bills with whatever money they have left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foot' looks like the verb, as in footing the bill; it is a unit of metre in verse.
explanation.definitionFit: In poetry a metrical unit of one unstressed then one stressed syllable is called an iamb.

clue.text: Small volume retailer unlikely to carry reserves

indicators.note: in a down entry, whatever is carried sits on top of the carrier, which fixes the order

parts.note: to reserve a table or seat is to book it
a tall story is an unlikely one

explanation.surface: A small shop selling low quantities is unlikely to keep stock in reserve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small volume' suggests low sales but means little books; 'reserves' looks like spare stock but is a verb meaning books.
explanation.definitionFit: A stand at a station or market selling printed reading matter is a small shop dealing in volumes.

clue.text: In report, SPECTRE assess move away from crime

indicators.note: a report is something spoken, so the words are taken by their sound

parts.note: a spectre is a ghost, and to assess is to rate

explanation.surface: A report says the villainous SPECTRE organisation, from the James Bond films, must reconsider its criminal ways.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make SPECTRE look like the Bond villains' organisation, but it is just a ghost; said quickly, ghost rate sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Going straight is an idiom for a former criminal turning honest and living within the law.

clue.text: Censure learner driver developing a taste for corners

indicators.note: to corner someone is to trap them, so one piece is enclosed by another

parts.note: taking to something is starting to like it
a learner driver displays an L plate

explanation.surface: A learner who has begun enjoying taking corners at speed gets told off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corners' looks like driving round bends; it is a verb meaning traps, with the second phrase trapping the L.
explanation.definitionFit: A talking-to is a scolding or reprimand, so it fits censure as a noun.

clue.text: Repetition of "wobble" in Just a Minute?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a wobble is a shake, so saying it again gives a pair of them

definitions.note: the idiom is 'in two shakes', so the answer stands for the phrase without 'in'
definitions.meaning: second meaning: an idiom for very soon

explanation.surface: A contestant on Just a Minute, the BBC radio panel game that penalises repetition, says 'wobble' twice.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals point to the radio show, where repeating a word loses points; read plainly, the words mean 'very shortly'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'in two shakes' is short for two shakes of a lamb's tail, meaning almost at once.

clue.text: Well contains dissolved chemical for sure

indicators.note: to contain is to hold inside, so one word wraps around another

parts.note: doing something well is doing it competently
a solute is the substance dissolved in a solution

explanation.surface: A water well is certainly holding some chemical in solution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well' looks like a source of water; it is the adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: Absolutely is an emphatic yes, meaning certainly, so it can replace the phrase in a reply.

clue.text: Hold long hairy creature

parts.note: to bear is to carry or support
to long for something is to be dying for it

explanation.surface: An order to keep hold of a long-haired animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long hairy' reads as one description, but 'long' is a verb, as in dying to do something.
explanation.definitionFit: A beardie is a bearded collie, a shaggy-coated sheepdog breed, so a very hairy animal.

clue.text: American sailors taking break for north wind to ease

indicators.note: a break is a gap opened up, and taking one in means holding a letter inside it

parts.note: US is the abbreviation for American
a crew is a ship's company
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: American seamen take a break when the north wind lets up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'North wind' reads as weather, but 'wind' starts the definition and rhymes with 'find'; 'break' tells N to split the first two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To unscrew is to turn a fastening so that it loosens, winding it to slacken it.

clue.text: Our last head of state quit because of that

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, was the previous British monarch
to go is to leave

explanation.surface: A British reader suggests the late Queen stepped down for a particular reason.
explanation.walkthrough: ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the cipher of Queen Elizabeth II, predecessor of the current king.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergo is Latin for therefore, used to introduce a conclusion drawn from what came before.

clue.text: Parent remains inside for wet spring again

parts.note: to parent a child is to rear it
something that remains still is, in the sense of continuing to exist

indicators.note: the inside of a short word is its middle, so only the central letter is kept

parts.note: the middle letter of the three

explanation.surface: A parent stays indoors during a rainy spring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wet spring' looks like the weather, but 'wet' supplies a letter and 'spring' belongs to the definition, used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To arise is to spring up, and the RE prefix makes it happen a second time.

clue.text: Desire urban speed limit reduced to protect society

indicators.note: protecting something means shielding it on all sides, so one letter sits inside
reduced means cut down, so the last letter is lopped off

parts.note: 30 mph is the usual speed limit in British towns
S is the abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: A campaign wants town speed limits lowered to keep the community safe.
explanation.walkthrough: Cut THIRTY to THIRT, then put S inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Thirst is a craving or longing, used figuratively as in a thirst for knowledge.

clue.text: Many minute noodles

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for minute
a noodle is a fool, as is an ass

explanation.surface: Lots of instant noodles, the kind ready in a minute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minute noodles' looks like a snack ready in a minute, but noodles here are fools.
explanation.definitionFit: Masses, as in 'masses of food', is an informal way of saying a great quantity or lots.

clue.text: Miles tossed his mother's hospital stuff in jumble

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for miles

indicators.note: tossed things are thrown about and land in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
Ma is mother, with the possessive s
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: Someone called Miles throws his mother's hospital things into a heap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miles' looks like a man's name; it is just M.
explanation.definitionFit: A mishmash is a confused mixture, a jumble of assorted stuff.

clue.text: Late caller whose features can't be distinguished?

definitions.note: a descriptive clause for a person rather than a noun

parts.note: the late So-and-so is a person who has died
one who rings, or calls, on the telephone

explanation.surface: A night-time visitor arrives whose face cannot be made out in the dark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' looks like the time of a visit; it means deceased. The definition is a description of someone who looks exactly like another person.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a person who looks exactly like someone else, so their faces cannot be told apart.

clue.text: Get a load of Sir Keir

indicators.note: a load of something is a portion of it, so the letters are a part of the phrase

parts.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: 'Get a load of him' — a jibe at Sir Keir Starmer, the British Prime Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get a load of' reads as one slang phrase meaning 'look at'; split it, and 'Get' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Get can mean annoy, as in 'it really gets me', which is the sense of irk.

clue.text: Large parts down there sound bull-like

indicators.note: to part something is to split it open, letting a letter sit between the halves

parts.note: below means further down
L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A rude remark about big body parts below the waist making a bovine noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parts' looks like a plural noun; it is the verb, splitting the second piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To bellow is to roar loudly and deeply, the noise a bull makes.

clue.text: Beneficial to lock building that should be secure

parts.note: something that is for you is good for you
a lock of hair is a tress

explanation.surface: A good lock is a help for a building that needs to be secure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lock' looks like a door fastening, apt beside 'secure'; it is a lock of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A fortress is a heavily fortified stronghold, designed above all to be safe from attack.
